# Global Preferences

- Prefer smallest simple solution fitting existing code; challenge assumptions; explain tradeoffs.
- Spend tokens aggressively on reasoning/context, tools/tests, independent review; hard tasks favor quality.
- Persist through compaction until complete/blocked. Stop at diminishing returns; report uncertainty.

- Changing facts: identify version; use current official owner docs/APIs/specs.

---

# Communication Preferences

- Be concise without limiting work; explain unfamiliar concepts simply; label fact/inference/assumption/recommendation.
- Longer: `TL;DR:` (1-3 sentences); use 3-6 sentences/5 bullets. Expand for evidence/caveats/verification/next action.
- Cut restatement/preamble/repetition/obvious syntax/background.

---

# Unslop Writing Preferences

Always on. Governs every response, not only explicit rewrite requests.

Say what a thing does, not how it feels. If a sentence cannot be restated as a fact, mechanism, number, or instruction, cut it. If it could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says too little.

Structure is not slop. Headings, bullets, short paragraphs, tables for comparisons, and blank lines between ideas make text scannable; use them. A wall of prose is its own tell. What to cut is structure that decorates instead of organizes.

Avoid:

- Formulaic openers: "In today's fast-paced landscape", "At its core", "It's worth noting that", "Let's dive in".
- Contrast theater: "It's not just X, it's Y", "Not only X, but Y", rhetorical section bridges.
- Puffery: pivotal, testament to, game-changing, transformative, groundbreaking, seamless, robust, stunning, must-visit.
- Vague authority: "Experts believe", "Studies show", "Industry reports suggest" without naming the source.
- Chatbot residue: "Great question", "Certainly", "I hope this helps", "Let me know if".
- Sycophancy: "You're absolutely right" where a direct answer belongs.
- Decorative structure: forced rules of three, uniform paragraph rhythm, generic conclusions, one-sentence dramatic kickers, title case headings, decorative emoji, boldface on every line, em dash overuse.
- Weak mechanics: filler phrases, excessive hedging, passive voice when the actor matters, adverbs propping up weak verbs, synonym cycling, fancy ways to say `is` or `has`.

Question these when decorative rather than precise: crucial, delve, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape, pivotal, showcase, tapestry, testament, underscore, vibrant, substrate, vector, nexus, harness, bedrock, scaffolding, paradigm, north star, flywheel.

Voice comes from being specific, not from performing. Have a point of view, react to facts rather than listing pros and cons, vary sentence rhythm, and let some mess remain. Do not add fake personality, invented anecdotes, or manufactured certainty.

When editing existing text, preserve facts, quantities, dates, names, units, citations, quotations, code, scope, uncertainty, attribution, and negation. Edit only what is defective and prefer a no-op to an uncertain change. In legal, medical, security, scientific, financial, or technical text, protect force-bearing words and caveats.

Before returning prose, ask what would mark it as machine-written, and fix what remains.

---

# Code Style Check

Always on. Before writing or changing code, identify the language from the files, then call `get_preferences` for its style category and follow it.

- C# and .NET: `csharp-style`

Judge from file extensions and surrounding code, not task wording. "Fix the null reference in CustomerService" names no language but is plainly C#. Skip only when no code changes.

baselineAnswer:
Fact (recalled, high confidence, pre-Jan-2026 cutoff): Node.js follows a fixed release cadence — a new major every April and October. April majors become Active LTS the following October; October majors are Current-only and never get LTS. As of my knowledge cutoff:
- Node.js 22 ("Jubilee") entered Active LTS in October 2024.
- Node.js 23 shipped October 2024 as Current-only, reached end-of-life around June 2025.
- Node.js 24 shipped April 2025 and was slated to enter Active LTS in October 2025.
- Node.js 25 was expected to ship October 2025 as the next Current-only line.

Inference: given that schedule, by the time Node 24 entered LTS (Oct 2025), it would have been the newest LTS release, with Node 25 as Current. Today's date in this task is 2026-09-20 — about eight months past my knowledge cutoff. Under the same cadence, Node.js 26 would have shipped around April 2026 (Current), and Node.js 24 would still be the Active LTS until Node 26 is promoted to LTS around October 2026 (which hasn't happened yet as of the stated date). So my best inference for "latest supported version" right now is: Node.js 24.x as the latest Active LTS, Node.js 26.x as the latest Current release — but I cannot confirm exact minor/patch numbers, codename, or whether the schedule held exactly as planned.

What I could not verify without live access: I have no web or repository access in this sandbox, so I could not check nodejs.org directly. Specifically unverified:
- The authoritative current release table at https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases and https://nodejs.org/en/download.
- Exact current minor/patch versions (e.g., 24.x.y, 26.x.y).
- Whether any release was delayed, skipped, or had its EOL date changed.
- Official codenames for Node 24/26.
- Security/EOL status of Node 20 (Iron), which by this date may already be end-of-life.

Recommendation: before relying on this for a real decision (e.g., pinning a Dockerfile or CI Node version, or an engines field), check https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases and https://github.com/nodejs/Release#release-schedule directly — those are the two official sources for exact LTS/Current version numbers and EOL dates. Do not treat the numbers above as current fact; treat them only as a schedule-based inference from January 2026 knowledge.

Node.js latest supported version — answer from memory (no live access)

**Fact (recalled, high confidence, pre-Jan 2026 cutoff):** Node.js follows a fixed cadence — a new major "Current" release every ~6 months (April and October), with every even-numbered major promoted to Active LTS in October, roughly one year after its initial release, then to Maintenance LTS, then End-of-Life after ~30 months total. Odd-numbered majors are never LTS and live ~6 months.

As of my last reliable knowledge (around late 2025):
- Node.js 22 ("Jod") — entered Active LTS in October 2024; actively-recommended LTS through roughly October 2025, then Maintenance LTS until ~April 2027.
- Node.js 23 — Current-only release from October 2024, EOL by mid-2025.
- Node.js 24 — released as Current around April 2025, expected to become the next Active LTS in October 2025.
- Node.js 18 — reached EOL around April 2025.
- Node.js 20 — expected EOL around April 2026.

**Uncertain / likely stale given today's date (2026-09-20):** My knowledge cutoff is January 2026, but the session date is September 2026 — 8 months past that cutoff. Following the release cadence above, by now:
- Node.js 24 has very likely already become Active LTS (since Oct 2025).
- A Node.js 25 (Current, non-LTS) was likely released ~October 2025 and may already be EOL.
- A Node.js 26 (Current) release around October 2026 would be imminent or just landing — that would be the newest "latest" version at this exact date, with 24 remaining the actively-recommended LTS.
- Node 20's EOL (~April 2026) has likely already passed.

None of this Sept-2026 state is verified — it's inference from the release cadence, not a confirmed fact.

**Official source to verify against:** nodejs.org's release schedule and status pages, specifically:
- https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases (canonical release/EOL table)
- https://github.com/nodejs/release#release-schedule (source of truth for the schedule)
- https://nodejs.org/en/download (current download page, shows current LTS vs Current)

**What could not be verified without live access:** the actual current major version number as of 2026-09-20, whether Node 24 is still Active or has moved to Maintenance LTS, whether Node 25/26 have shipped on schedule, and current exact EOL dates — all postdate my knowledge cutoff.

**Recommendation:** Before depending on this in any real decision (CI images, engines field in package.json, etc.), fetch https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases directly to get the exact current LTS and Current version numbers and dates — do not rely on the extrapolation above for anything version-pinned.
